summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a web app built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It answers one question for any place and date on the Moon: will a lander have sunlight for power, and can it talk to Earth?

Users pick a site or click anywhere on an interactive 3D Moon built from NASA LRO LOLA terrain and imagery. The app shows when the Sun and Earth rise and set above the real mountain horizon, how much solar power is available, and how long the longest night lasts. "Stand here" puts you on the surface to watch the Sun skim the ridges near the south pole.

Three levels of detail (Explore, Compare and Expert) serve the public, educators and mission planners. Sun and Earth positions match NASA JPL Horizons to within 0.003°, and everything runs offline in the browser.
details:
What it does / how it works

Lunar Landing Site Navigator answers one question for any place and date on the Moon: will a lander have sunlight for power, and can it talk to Earth? Users pick a landing site (Apollo, CLPS, Artemis III regions) or click anywhere on an interactive 3D Moon.

The app calculates where the Sun and Earth are relative to the real terrain horizon, built from NASA LOLA elevation data. From that it shows:

  • when the Sun and Earth rise and set
  • the solar power available right now
  • the share of the month with Earth in view
  • the longest night a lander must survive

“Stand here” puts you on the surface to watch the Sun skim the polar mountains.

Benefits

  • Turns information spread across Quickmap, Moon Trek and JPL Horizons into an answer in seconds.
  • Mission planners can re-check a site when a launch slips, compare sites and dates side by side, and search nearby terrain for a sunnier spot.

Intended impact

  • Faster landing-site decisions for missions near the south pole.
  • A clear, visual way for educators and the public to understand why Artemis is going to the south pole, and why that’s hard.

Tools

  • TypeScript, React and Vite for the app; CesiumJS for the 3D globe; Web Workers for heavy computation.
  • astronomy-engine for Sun and Earth positions, checked against NASA JPL Horizons (accurate to 0.003°).
  • NASA data: LRO LOLA terrain, LROC imagery (CGI Moon Kit) and NSSDC landing-site records.
  • Node.js scripts to process the data. No special hardware needed: it runs in any modern browser.

Creativity

  • A first-person “Stand here” view lit by the real Sun.
  • A time slider that plays a month like a video.
  • Three detail levels in one app (Explore, Compare, Expert).
  • Plain-English answers with green, amber and red ratings.

Factors considered

  • Accuracy: checked against JPL Horizons.
  • Ease of use: usable at every skill level.
  • Speed: no waiting on the network for answers.
  • Reliability: works offline, with no server or API keys.
  • Openness about limits: the terrain is 240 m resolution, and approximate Artemis III points are labelled as such.
